data.text/html:
Hypothesis testing, explained interactively

An interactive companion to DataMListic's video "Hypothesis Testing - Explained".One-line framing: a hypothesis test is a trial. You assume the boring explanation is true, then ask whether the evidence is too surprising to keep believing it. We follow the video's chapters and its running example: a factory claims its light bulbs last 1,000 hours on average. We test 36 bulbs, the known standard deviation is σ = 50, and we measure x̄ = 985.
Chapter What you'll touch
1 · The courtroom Choose the verdict rules
2 · The null world A bulb-factory simulator that builds the null distribution of x̄
3 · The test statistic A draggable z-ruler: move x̄ and read off z
4 · The p-value Shaded tails that follow your drag
5 · The decision Run 2,000 trials and count Type I and Type II errors
6 · The whole picture Drag the alternative world and watch the power grow
(The companion notebook p_values.py covers how to interpret p-values and the problem of p-hacking. Here we focus on how a test is put together.) Colour language (used everywhere): ■ blue = the null world (H₀) · ■ orange = the alternative world (H₁) · ■ red = the rejection region / α · ■ green = power · ■ purple = your observed data

data.text/markdown:
1 · The courtroom

"A defendant walks into a courtroom. The court doesn't start by asking 'Is this person guilty?' It starts with a presumption: innocent until proven guilty."
Courtroom Hypothesis test Bulb example
Innocent (presumed) Null hypothesis H₀ ||(\mu = 1000||) h (the factory's claim)
Guilty Alternative hypothesis H₁ ||(\mu \neq 1000||) h
Evidence Sample data → test statistic 36 bulbs, ||(\bar x = 985||)
"Beyond reasonable doubt" Significance level α usually 0.05
Convict Reject H₀
Acquit Fail to reject H₀ (never "accept H₀")
The burden of proof is on the evidence. We start by assuming H₀ is true and only abandon it if the data would be very surprising in that world.

Which pair of verdicts did the court actually choose between?\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-options='["Guilty or not guilty","Guilty or innocent"]' data-inline='false' data-disabled='false'></marimo-radio></marimo-ui-element>

data.text/markdown: Pick one above.

2 · The null world

If H₀ is true, every bulb comes from a factory with mean ||(\mu_0 = 1000||) and ||(\sigma = 50||). We never see one bulb at a time. We see the average of 36. The central limit theorem says that average is approximately normal: ||[\bar X \;\overset{H_0}{\sim}\; \mathcal N\!\left(\mu_0,\ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right),\qquad \text{SE} = \frac{50}{\sqrt{36}} = 8.33 \text{ h}||]This bell curve is "what the world looks like if H₀ is true", the null world. Below, the factory makes batches of bulbs. Each batch of n bulbs (purple ticks) becomes one dot in the histogram of x̄. The blue curve is the CLT prediction. Even single bulbs from a skewed factory produce a bell-shaped x̄.

data.text/markdown: Press ▶ play or +500 tests above. Stats appear here every 20 tests.

Does the purple histogram fit the blue curve? About how often does an \u003cem\u003ehonest\u003c/em\u003e factory give x̄ ≤ 985?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003cstrong\u003en = 4\u003c/strong\u003e. The null world gets wider, so 985 is no longer unusual. Set \u003cstrong\u003en = 100\u003c/strong\u003e. Now 985 sits in the far tail.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSwitch to the \u003cstrong\u003eskewed\u003c/strong\u003e bulb shape with n = 1, then with n = 36. Single bulbs are lopsided, but averages of 36 still form a bell. That is the CLT at work.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3 · The test statistic: a ruler for surprise

Is 985 far from 1000? A 15-hour gap could be huge or tiny. It depends on how much x̄ normally wobbles. So we measure the gap in units of standard error. That ruler is the z-score: ||[z = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt n} = \frac{985 - 1000}{50/\sqrt{36}} = \frac{-15}{8.33} = -1.80||]"Our sample mean sits 1.8 standard errors below the claimed average." Drag the purple marker below. The top axis is in hours, and the bottom ruler is in z (standard errors). Notice that z sees the hours only through the SE: change n and the same 985 h lands on a different z.

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='iLit-0' random-id='8c4fa31a-09da-5d97-4d36-48adf20796e0'><marimo-anywidget data-initial-value='{"model_id":"0f0cc80726e84e4798e627d35907b8aa"}' data-label='null' data-model-id='"0f0cc80726e84e4798e627d35907b8aa"'></marimo-anywidget></marimo-ui-element>

data.text/markdown: ||[z = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n} = \frac{985.0 - 1000}{50/\sqrt{36}} = \frac{-15.0}{8.33} = \mathbf{-1.80}||]Your x̄ sits 1.80 standard errors below the claimed mean.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eLeave the marker at \u003cstrong\u003e985\u003c/strong\u003e and slide \u003cstrong\u003en\u003c/strong\u003e from 4 to 144. The gap in hours stays the same, but \u003cem\u003ez\u003c/em\u003e grows like √n.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eFind the x̄ that sits exactly on the red line for n = 36 and α = 0.05. You should get about 1000 − 1.96 × 8.33 ≈ \u003cstrong\u003e983.7 h\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSwitch H₁ to \u003cstrong\u003eleft (μ &lt; 1000)\u003c/strong\u003e. Now only \u003cem\u003elow\u003c/em\u003e lifetimes count as evidence, and the single red line moves to −1.645.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · The p-value: how likely is data this extreme, if H₀ is true?

Shade every z that is at least as extreme as yours, in the null world. That shaded area is the p-value: ||[p = P\big(|Z| \ge |z_{\text{obs}}| \;\big|\; H_0\big) = 2\,\Phi(-|z_{\text{obs}}|) \quad\text{(two-sided)}||]For the bulbs, ||(p = 2\Phi(-1.80) \approx 0.072||): "a 7.2% chance of seeing data this extreme if the null hypothesis is actually true." The purple area in the ruler above is this number. (For pitfalls in reading p-values, see the companion p_values.py notebook.) Predict first: before you look, guess the p-value for z = −2.5 (two-sided).
Make your guess, then lock it in.

data.text/html: Reference table. A one-sided p is half the two-sided p, because only one tail counts.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag x̄ back to 985 (n = 36, two-sided). Check that the readout says \u003cstrong\u003ep ≈ 0.072\u003c/strong\u003e, the number from the video.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSwitch to \u003cstrong\u003eleft (μ &lt; 1000)\u003c/strong\u003e. The same data now gives p ≈ 0.036 &lt; 0.05. The choice of H₁ has to be made \u003cstrong\u003ebefore\u003c/strong\u003e you see the data, or this becomes a way to cheat.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag the marker \u003cem\u003eto the right\u003c/em\u003e while the test is left-sided. p climbs toward 1, because high lifetimes are no evidence that bulbs fail \u003cem\u003eearly\u003c/em\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · The decision, and the two ways to be wrong

We need "a line in the sand": the significance level α (usually 0.05). ||[\text{if } p < \alpha \Rightarrow \text{reject } H_0 \qquad\qquad \text{if } p \ge \alpha \Rightarrow \text{fail to reject } H_0||]For the bulbs, ||(0.072 \ge 0.05||), so we fail to reject. "The data is a bit suspicious, but not suspicious enough." But you can always be wrong:
H₀ true (innocent) H₁ true (guilty)
Reject H₀ (convict) ❌ Type I error, false positive, rate = α ✅ correct, rate = power
Fail to reject (acquit) ✅ correct, rate = 1 − α ❌ Type II error, false negative, rate = β
Below we run 2,000 independent bulb tests in a world you choose, and count the verdicts. (This uses α and the sidedness from section 3.)

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eKeep \u003cstrong\u003eμ = 1000\u003c/strong\u003e (H₀ true). About α × 2000 ≈ 100 tests still reject, purely by chance. \u003cem\u003e\"Alpha controls the Type I error rate: the probability of convicting an innocent null.\"\u003c/em\u003e The p-values are spread \u003cstrong\u003euniformly\u003c/strong\u003e from 0 to 1.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003cstrong\u003eμ = 985\u003c/strong\u003e, the video's sample mean, as if it were the truth. With n = 36, fewer than half of the tests catch it. Most guilty factories walk free. That is a high \u003cstrong\u003eType II\u003c/strong\u003e rate.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eKeep μ = 985 and raise \u003cstrong\u003en\u003c/strong\u003e to 144. Power climbs toward 1. Then lower α to 0.01 in section 3. Fewer false alarms, but more misses.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · The whole picture: two overlapping worlds

Put the null distribution of z (blue) next to a world where H₁ is true (orange), which is shifted by ||[\delta = \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}.||]
  • Red tails under blue: the rejection region, with total area α, beyond ±1.96 for α = 0.05.
  • Green under orange: the part of the alternative that lands in the rejection region. That is the power, ||(1-\beta||).
  • Faded orange under orange: the alternative falls in the "fail to reject" zone. That is β, the Type II error rate.
"The overlap between these two curves is where mistakes happen." Drag the orange curve sideways.

Power drops to α: when the worlds coincide, \"rejecting\" is just a false alarm.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag to \u003cstrong\u003eδ ≈ 2.8\u003c/strong\u003e. Power ≈ 0.80, the usual design target. \u003cem\u003e\"The further apart these two curves sit, the easier it is to tell them apart.\"\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eLower \u003cstrong\u003eα\u003c/strong\u003e to 0.01. The red tails shrink, and so does the green area. Fewer Type I errors cost you Type II errors. Look at the power-vs-n chart to see how many more bulbs it takes to win the power back.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
7 · Sandbox: run your own test, start to finish

Make up any factory, then draw a fresh sample of bulbs and walk through the five steps from the video: hypotheses → null world → test statistic → p-value → decision. If you set the true μ yourself, you also know whether the verdict was right, which is something a real analyst never gets to know.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eChallenges\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet true μ = μ₀ and click 🎲 twenty times. How many false alarms do you get at α = 0.05? (You should expect about 1.)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eWith true μ = 990 and σ = 50, find the smallest n where most of your rolls reject. Compare it with the power chart in section 6.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet σ = 5. Now even a 1-hour difference is detected easily. A tiny SE makes \u003cem\u003etrivial\u003c/em\u003e gaps \"significant\".\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
8 · Quiz: put the framework to work

Answer all six, then flip the reveal switch.
Answered 0/6. Flip the switch when you're ready.

Recap

Step (video chapter) Idea Formula / rule Where you touched it
The courtroom Presume H₀ ("innocent"), require evidence to reject H₀: μ = μ₀, H₁: μ ≠ μ₀ §1 verdict check
The null world The distribution of the statistic if H₀ is true ||(\bar X \sim \mathcal N(\mu_0, \sigma/\sqrt n)||) (CLT) §2 bulb-factory simulator
The test statistic A ruler for surprise, in standard errors ||(z = (\bar x-\mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)||) §3 draggable z-ruler
The p-value Chance of data at least this extreme under H₀ ||(p = 2\Phi(-\lvert z\rvert)||) (two-sided) §4 shaded tails, predict-then-reveal
The decision Compare with α; never "accept" H₀ reject if ||(p<\alpha||) §5 2,000 trials
Errors Type I = false positive (rate α), Type II = false negative (rate β) §5 verdict counts
The whole picture Power = rejection-region area under H₁ ||(1-\beta = \Phi(\delta - z_{\alpha/2}) + \Phi(-\delta - z_{\alpha/2})||) §6 draggable alternative
Bulb example, final numbers: SE = 8.33 h, z = −1.80, p ≈ 0.072 > 0.05, so we fail to reject. If the true mean really were 985 h, a 36-bulb test would catch it only about 44% of the time. Next: p_values.py covers what a p-value is not, and how p-hacking breaks the α guarantee you saw in section 5.
